I wanna make sure I understand what you're saying or I'm thinking about the right implications going forward. I mean, in Q4, you guys had a big CapEx that came in a lot higher than expected. You pre-released that. We got another one here this quarter. If I understood you correctly, the two main drivers appear to be increased cycle time or reduced cycle time, so increased pace, and a higher oil price, which leads to more AFE proposals. If that's correct, what is your, are those two vectors, are they flat going forward?
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
I'm not sure I follow, Charles.
Charles Meade
Managing Director and Large Cap Exploration and Production Research Analyst, Johnson Rice and Company
I mean, if those are the two big drivers, you know, you can go a different direction if you want. The question is, as we look at Q2 and Q3, are those arrows still pointed up? Are we gonna have further decreased cycle times?
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
I mean, yeah, I think.
Charles Meade
Managing Director and Large Cap Exploration and Production Research Analyst, Johnson Rice and Company
Maybe the oil price isn't going up, but perhaps, you know, is there a building wave of AFEs, or is this kind of a spurt that's gonna attend to that?
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
I got a question in, like, 2018 when I first started here being like, okay, you know, is the productivity improvement in the Bakken done? Because, you know, well costs, you know, wells have gotten so much better and fracking's gotten so much better. Then every single year, they found ways to make wells better. I got the same question last year, and I got the same question the year before. The answer is, the industry is amazing. They found ways to go faster and faster and faster. Frankly, you know, the onus is on us.
Look, we have candidly struggled to keep up with the pace, and we've been. I mean, I don't view it necessarily as a bad thing, but the speed at which our operators have gone has obviously taken us by surprise to some degree. At the same time, like, I just. I don't really see this as necessarily the total catastrophe. Like, you can see it in our weighted average cost of a well. We're not blowing through, we're not having inflationary pressures. If you look at the overall capital delta, we drilled 3 extra wells this quarter, right? You saw it in the top line results, right? I don't. Again, like, I don't really see a major disconnect here.
The delta last quarter is masked by the fact that ultimately it's really a percentage of completion thing as opposed to additional wells. Ultimately, you're seeing cycle times. Can I predict if the operators are gonna stop going faster? I don't know if I can make that prediction because that would be predicting something that I don't control. I would say operators are incentivized to make more and more money. I'd say whether oil prices are going up or down, I'd say if oil prices go down, they're gonna still try to find a way to make more money. They're gonna find a way to go faster and faster and make more money. I would say no, they're gonna still find ways to go faster.
Adam Dirlam
President, Northern Oil and Gas
It's just gonna depend on the operator mix and the development mix and the working interest that we're getting in the door, right? You don't necessarily have that view with AFEs because they might ballot two AFEs, you know, one week, and then they follow it up with six more, and they all end up being on the same path. Those are things that we need to digest and, you know, truly understand. I think the AFE activity has picked up. We've seen that in March and April, and, you know, we would expect that, you know, in this environment, all things remaining the same, that, you know, development cadence and everything else will continue. That can change on a dime.
Charles Meade
Managing Director and Large Cap Exploration and Production Research Analyst, Johnson Rice and Company
Got it. Thank you for that.
Operator
Question comes from the line of Derrick Whitfield of Stifel. Please go ahead.
Derrick Whitfield
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Stifel
Thanks. Good morning, all.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Good morning.
Derrick Whitfield
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Stifel
Regarding the larger asset packages, how would you characterize the competition you're experiencing in that market at present? Aside from the quality and wider bid-ask spreads you saw in Q1, is that still a robust market and opportunity for you?
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah. I mean, we haven't. It's a larger package, Derek. I don't think we felt like there's a ton of. I mean, we've certainly seen bankers give the illusion of competition in a couple cases, but we haven't really seen much competition in reality. I think where the challenge has been more that there's been a, of late, it's been harder for us to find assets that we've really wanted to lean in on, meaning like where you knew the clearing price and would we really feel like they were assets that we would be willing to pay what you knew it was required to take it home, I guess, is where I was.
Adam Dirlam
President, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah. Framed it up a different way for you. I mean, we're certainly seeing more entrants from, you know, family offices, some private equity groups and, you know, some crossover from the minerals side, which is obviously validating in terms of other sources recognizing the power of the business model. That's largely limited to smaller funds. Where I think you're seeing maybe a little bit more of an elevation in competition is on the smaller ground game side.
We're just playing in different sandboxes when you're starting to talk about asset packages that are north of $150 million in terms of funds that are being raised and being able to handle, you know, potential concentration, those types of things. I think, you know, what we're seeing in that regard is generally status quo. Obviously, that can also change, but based on kind of what we're seeing and the feedback that we're getting, I don't see a material change on the large.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah. I mean, I'd say.
Adam Dirlam
President, Northern Oil and Gas
Large scale.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
I'd say where we see people. We've definitely seen buyers of PDP-centric assets, and...
Adam Dirlam
President, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
... That's where we're very happy to see that because that's just not where we're generally focused.
Adam Dirlam
President, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah. I mean, from time to time, I think we see some groups that raise capital and deploy it in a meaningful way. There was, you know, one group that we saw ended up paying north of 75% of where we were coming out at. We're happy to let them have it. Frankly, they shot their one and only bullet, and we haven't heard from them again. They can digest that as long as they need to. Then if they wanna sell it, then maybe at that point, it's worth taking another look at it, but not at those prices.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah. I mean, I just, I would just tell you this. I don't think there's been an asset that we've coveted yet that we really felt was very attractive to us, that we haven't felt that we were outmatched for, you know, when we've really, you know, of the quality that you've seen us execute on, where we've really had to stretch or, you know, go out of our comfort zone for. I think that that's a testament to where we are in the marketplace.
Derrick Whitfield
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Stifel
Terrific. As my follow-up, really thinking about Permian macro regarding the pipeline outages and tighter egress conditions that are expected until Matterhorn comes on in Q3.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah.
Derrick Whitfield
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Stifel
Are you guys expecting industry to adjust turn in line activity to match supply growth with egress growth?
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah. Yeah. I mean, you're definitely seeing, you know, especially for some of the smaller operators, they're having to navigate around it. I mean, I think we're blessed with the fact that most of our operators in the Permian are, you know, bigger operators with more integrated midstream systems and better access points. Even they have to navigate around these issues, Derek. It's not a small issue, and I don't wanna sugarcoat it. You can see that. I think we for better or for worse, and I would like to say we were geniuses, but we basically have almost zero Waha exposure this year, you know, financially speaking at least. We effectively hedged all of it away.
I'd love to say we did it completely, you know, on purpose, but we just really were a little bit concerned coming into the year, and I think we just had a heavy hand on it when we were hedging it and partly because we were so acquisitive last year. I think that it's gonna take some time. I mean, some of it is as you rightly highlight, some of it is it's been made worse by maintenance, but I don't think it's necessarily gonna get, you know, magically better this year. Next year, I don't think it. I think it's still gonna be a wide issue for some time. I think it's gonna take a couple of years, and you're gonna need more and more to be built out. I do think it's going to limit some growth, particularly in the Delaware, for the next year or so.
Derrick Whitfield
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Stifel
Makes sense. Very helpful.
Operator
Your next question comes from the line of Donovan Schafer of Northland Capital. Please go ahead.
Donovan Schafer
Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Northland Capital Markets
Hey, guys. Thanks for taking the questions. I wanna ask about, and I know we've already had a couple of people ask about the better than expected well performance. This might feel like beating a dead horse, but I kinda wanna get to the core of it. In the sense of, like, to what extent should we care? If we just talk, let's forget about the wells being pulled forward or whatever. If we're just talking about, like, for a given well, the performance of that well versus your own expectations, if we just focus on that, you know, and you said, I think, you know, Nick, you said it's flat out better well performance.
Who gets sort of the credit for that? Is it just a chance phenomenon and it just, you know, you just there's a statistical distribution and it just happens to be that, you know, the rolls of the dice were better this time around? Was it, you know, can you identify changes in sort of well design, or do you feel like the strength of particular operators, or is it alternatively like an, you know, a matter of conservative underwriting? Like, another way to put it is should this be seen as an achievement of some kind, somehow tied to, you know, like, human agency? Is this just a matter of chance? If it's some sort of, like, achievement, you know, who gets that credit? Is it a reflection of your business model? Is it a reflection of your operators? Yeah, that would be really great.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
I mean, I think I would certainly wanna give credit to the operators for their great performance. I mean, certainly they do all the hard work, and I don't wanna not give credit where credit's due. To our engineering team, you know, we work really hard to set a standard and underwrite accordingly and then try to meet and beat those expectations. I think that, you know, then obviously for you guys to underpromise and overdeliver. It's not to lowball or anything like that, but, you know, you really do. This is a risky business, right? It is a risky business, and I think the oil and gas business is filled with optimists, right?
I always joke that as a non-operator, you really need to be pessimistic because there are. You find out that many operators, you know, they make a change in well design and they say, see better IPs, and they carry it forward and think everything is gonna be better. They do one refrac is good, and they think all refracs are gonna be better, and it turns out that it's locational, right? We try really hard to take a skeptical lens and be conservative about this. I think that's why generally our reserves have been conservative, and we tend to do well. I wanna give a lot of credit to our team that we tend to see better, you know, better results than not.
It also, you know, it comes down to a philosophy, and I talk about this in my prepared comments of assets and operators, which is that you can't engineer bad assets, which is that you can try to pay, you know, a high discount rate for really bad assets, but at the end of the day, those assets aren't gonna be resilient. When I was a stock analyst back in the day, I would always rather pay a premium for a really good management team and a really good company than, you know, pay a low price for a really bad stock.
Because the chances were over time, that bad stock or that cheap stock, something bad was gonna happen because it was a bad company, and it was not gonna be resilient. It goes the same thing for oil and gas assets, which is that you buy really high quality reservoirs and really high quality operators, and chances are they're going to do good things with them. I think that that's what our team really focuses on here, which is that you focus on the best operators in the best areas, and you tend to be pleasantly surprised. I don't know, Jim, if you wanna add to that.
Jim Evans
CTO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah. I think the other thing you think about too is operators are always trying to innovate and be more efficient. It's not just about getting more EUR, more reserves out of it, they're also trying to optimize their artificial lift operations. That's constantly changing, and we're constantly updating our type curves based on what the operators are doing. Some of it is they're just getting oil out faster, right? It's not necessarily that they're gonna get more EUR over the life of it. They've just found a way to get more out more efficiently, you know, through the first 12 to 18 months, which is a big driver of NPV and IRR, which is what we want. We're constantly taking that into account.
Like Nick said, you know, we wanna make sure that more often than not that the wells outperform versus underperform. That's just part of our culture here of how we look at things. We do constant look-backs on performance, you know, how wells are doing versus what we originally underwrote. Over the last three or four years, we've been less than 5% off in terms of that. We feel very confident about our underwriting here. This is just kind of a pleasant surprise by some of our operators in really good areas, and they found a way to just do better than what we had expected.
Donovan Schafer
Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Northland Capital Markets
Okay, great. Thank you. That is very helpful. Then as a follow-up. Nick, in your prepared remarks, you called out, and I thought this was kind of a good thing to call out and kind of a good insight, the potential for increased volatility. You're talking about with respect to your own positioning as a company and the importance of kind of financial flexibility because volatility, you know, it gives you different levers or things to pull or opens up opportunities. I'm curious kinda just specifically, 'cause I think you were saying, you know, well, with such low gas prices and also I think maybe you mentioned just that it's an election year or maybe it's just other, just sort of the geopolitical dynamics or whatever.
It does seem like a setup that we could see more volatility, you know, between now and November, December. I'm curious, were you specifically talking about like in terms of thinking about what might happen with your own, you know, with the volatility on stock and like other securities you could potentially bring in? Are you talking more broadly like, commodity prices as well and the potential for any type of wild swings around anything like that could like, just I wanna be clear 'cause I thought that was a-
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah
Donovan Schafer
Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Northland Capital Markets
A good point.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
I mean.
Donovan Schafer
Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Northland Capital Markets
I'm just curious what you're thinking. What things are the volatility you're talking about? Price, commodities, stocks, bonds, all of it?
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah, I mean, I think volatility means volatility. I think that, if you look at our track record over the last couple of years, we've bought our bonds, we've bought our stock, we have bought assets, right? We've bought gas assets, we've bought oil assets. We've done a lot of weird things during periods, you know, we buy. We spent $200 million buying distressed assets during 2020. Right? It was 90% of our capital, you know, our organic capital basically went to zero during 2020, right? I think during the if there are periods, you wanna be in a position, you know, to be able to act if, you know, extreme events happen.
Now, obviously if you're at an extreme point in natural gas spot pricing, I'm not sure you're at an extreme point in terms of the strip or in terms of asset pricing or you haven't seen, you know, distress certainly in natural gas for the assets themselves necessarily yet. I think the overall market, you know, to the extent we see a change in the interest rate cycle or things like that, we could definitely see things happen. I think, you know, we have to see what happens with the overall economy. Yeah, it is an election year and, typically you can see, you know, changes in policy and other things that could potentially happen. I think we just always wanna be in a position to act.
I always use that term dynamic, and I think it's because we wanna have the flexibility to make changes to those decisions. That's why, having a business, you know, walk softly and carry a big stick, right? To have that cash flow, to be able to make those dynamic decisions and make changes, you know, we've been able to buy our bonds in the low nineties. Now they trade, you know, at well north of par, right? You have those abilities to make good decisions when the market gives them to you.
Donovan Schafer
Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Northland Capital Markets
Okay. Very helpful. Thank you, guys.
Operator
Your next question comes from the line of Lloyd Byrne of Jefferies. Please go ahead.
Lloyd Byrne
Managing Director and Head of North American Energy Research, Jefferies
Hey, guys. Thanks for all the info. Let me come about the CapEx differently. It seems like there's a lot of concern, but if I look at the CapEx versus the bills, it feels like the AFEs are either in line or coming down, and maybe you can comment on that. Then also, you talked about a little bit of the deflation at Mascot and Novo, so maybe you can just comment on that as well.
Adam Dirlam
President, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah. Hey, Lloyd, this is Adam. I made some comments in my prepared remarks. We're definitely seeing it, you know, across the board, both from an absolute and, you know, normalized on a lateral foot basis. We've certainly seen that with our Mascot assets as well as our Novo assets. I think that's both a function of what we're seeing in terms of, you know, drilling, as well as just kind of spud to TIL timing as well. I think, you know, some of the tangibles, casing, those types of things are still pretty sticky. Operators are doing a pretty good job of being able to kinda pick away around the edges, and we see that persisting.
Lloyd Byrne
Managing Director and Head of North American Energy Research, Jefferies
Okay, thanks. Hey, Nick, just remind us more free cash flow coming forward, debt targets?
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah. I mean, we still target around 1x.
Lloyd Byrne
Managing Director and Head of North American Energy Research, Jefferies
Mm-hmm.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
I think we were about 1.1 last quarter. We're about just over 1.2 this quarter, and that's just a function that we closed our Northern Delaware acquisition. We did that. We should see, you know, absent any material change, and again, we're already close to May here, a material step-down this quarter again, you know, absent some unforeseen change in commodity prices over the next couple of months. Just given the fact that CapEx is scheduled to step down some, so we should see a material step-down in the revolver balances in Q2.
Lloyd Byrne
Managing Director and Head of North American Energy Research, Jefferies
Awesome.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
We expect we should be right back on the trend within Q2.
Lloyd Byrne
Managing Director and Head of North American Energy Research, Jefferies
Thank you, guys.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah.
Operator
Your next question comes from the line of Paul Diamond of Citi. Please go ahead.
Paul Diamond
VP and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Thank you. Good morning. Thanks for taking my call. Just a quick one on the M&A or purchase cadence. You had a pretty good clip in Q1. Are you seeing the same type of opportunity given current you know current pricing levels and you know as you look forward through what's expected to be a relatively volatile period in the market?
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah. I mean, there's certainly no shortage of opportunities. I think it's always about balancing the risk here, right? It's just about, you know, I think I would just tell you, I think the lower the price goes, I think our risk appetite increases. I think the higher the price of oil goes, probably the more wary we're going to become. You have sort of a, I'd say from a $65 to $85 range, you know, is probably a better range than above those. I'd say below $70, I think you're gonna find that sellers are probably gonna dry up because they're gonna feel that they're not getting good value for their assets. I think that, you know, in that range, that's sort of a good enough environment from a pricing perspective.
I think that we're in a relatively decent market. I think that again, the beginning of the year is always kind of a tricky. If you look at our pattern, generally, we've done less M&A in the H1 of any year, historically speaking, for whatever reason. It's just if you go back historically speaking, we've done very little stuff in the calendar going back the entirety of my time here. It tends to be something that happens towards the middle or the H2 of the year. Stay tuned. I do think that we're not short opportunities. I can tell you that much, Adam.
Adam Dirlam
President, Northern Oil and Gas
No, I mean, I think you nailed it. I think it's a function of you know, banks and you know, organizations bringing these packages to market and you know, what the lead time is on a lot of that stuff. You've got you know, the smaller competition kinda coming in with a bullish view on oil pricing, which creates some volatility in terms of the you know, the ground game. What I'd say, I mean, even just looking at some of our April activities, we've been making some pretty strong headway in that regard, being able to pick things up across you know, all three of our respective basins.
Then to Nick's point, it's really just gonna be a balance of what that quality looks like. Seller expectations and you know, expectations can be wildly different, especially in a volatile you know, commodity environment. If we're bouncing along at, you know, relatively static pricing for an extended period of time, that generally level sets expectations and narrows that bid-ask spread. If you have a material step up or a material step down in the short term, that's gonna just widen it.
Paul Diamond
VP and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Understood. Thanks for the clarity. Just a quick follow-up. You've talked pretty at length about the productivity improvements on the oil side. I mean, or where does your perspective sit on the nat gas side of it? I know it's a much smaller perspective or a much smaller piece.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah.
Paul Diamond
VP and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Just going forward, should we expect to see the, you know, kind of a similar cadence in your view?
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah, I mean, I would just say, like, I mean, I just tell you from my perspective, and I'm not the engineer here, but our Marcellus assets have outperformed really from the get-go. They have outperformed our internal modeling literally every quarter since we've owned them. Literally, I think there's not a month, and Jim tell me I'm wrong, but
Paul Diamond
VP and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Mm-hmm.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
They have done an excellent job. I mean, I think we've had a little bit less development than we had initially modeled, but the decline rates have been shallower. They've just consistently outperformed. I mean, it no wonder gas is $1.80, right? Because they just simply don't decline. I don't know if you wanna add to that.
Jim Evans
CTO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah, that's right. EQT, they completely changed the design of these wells from when we originally bought the asset. They've widened the spacing, changed the completion design, changed the pull back methodology. These wells just continue to hang in much better than we had expected. Obviously there's not a ton of activity that's been happening out there. Our modeling is still kind of based on old methodology, and we continue to update that as we go and we see more. Yeah, like Nick said, the Marcellus stuff just continues to outperform, and you know, the Utica beat in Q1 as well. Those wells continue to clean out better than we had expected. That was a nice outperformance there as well.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah. I mean, while it's not huge for us, if you actually model out our Appalachian asset and just how much cash flow it has generated for us over the life of its ownership, it has been an amazing investment for us. It is paid out in less than a year and then just continues, for very little capital investment, even with low gas prices to generate significant cash flow for us. It's been a great investment.
Paul Diamond
VP and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Understood. Thanks for the clarity.
Operator
Your next question comes from the line of Noel Parks of Tuohy Brothers. Please go ahead.
Noel Parks
Managing Director and Energy Research Analyst, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
Hi, good morning. I was wondering, do you have any sense of maybe where incremental service cost trends are heading in your basins? Feel like so far in earnings season, we've been getting sort of a mixed picture just depending on location and type of service. Any thoughts yet would be great.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
I would say, no, very modest deflation we've seen year to date, but I would imagine, you know, as oil prices have increased, I would guess that's a flattening trend.
Noel Parks
Managing Director and Energy Research Analyst, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
Okay. Great. Fair enough. I was just wondering, you did mention what we've all seen with, you know, gas in the Permian and so forth. I believe over time, you've discussed that you are pretty vigilant about the state of infrastructure when you're looking at potential deals out there and look to steer clear of areas where you have any questions or doubts. I'm just wondering, are you getting deals brought to you that fall into that category these days?
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah, yeah. I mean, I think a lot of the, you know, specifically a lot of assets in parts of the Delaware, you have to be very wary around, you know, particularly as you get, you know, in parts of New Mexico and other parts where they might be cringy. They may not have access to midstream systems, and you have to understand that going into it. You need to know who your operator is. Absolutely, I mean, all of that goes into the equation. You need to know who your operator is. Do they have, you know, firm access? Are they interruptible? Can they be kicked off the system? All that stuff.
That's why we tend to, you know, you hear us talk a lot about this, but knowing who your operator is, knowing what kind of, you know, midstream access they're gonna have is critical. I think, you know, as an issue overall, I think it's something that, you know, it's the Permian Basin, so, you know, it will over time get solved, but I think it's going to be chronic for some time. In the end, it's a minor economic annoyance, meaning it doesn't really destroy overall the wells. It just is something that we can model in and still make the wells economic, but it certainly doesn't help.
Adam Dirlam
President, Northern Oil and Gas
That's right. You just need to make sure that you're modeling it.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah. Right. I mean.
Adam Dirlam
President, Northern Oil and Gas
From a cost as well as a development timing standpoint.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Yeah. I mean, if we were trying to buy something in Alpine High or something like that, it might be a different equation, but that's not what...
Noel Parks
Managing Director and Energy Research Analyst, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
Great. Thanks a lot.
Operator
That concludes our Q&A session. I will now turn the conference back over to Nick O'Grady for closing remarks.
Nick O'Grady
CEO, Northern Oil and Gas
Thank you all for joining us today. We appreciate your continued support and look forward to touching base with you in the coming weeks.
Operator
Ladies and gentlemen, that concludes this call. Thank you all for joining. You may now disconnect.

content.text:
Evelyn Infurna
VP of Investor Relations, NOG
Good morning. Welcome to NOG's Q4 and year-end 2023 earnings conference call. Yesterday, after the close, we released our financial results for the Q4 and full year. You can access our earnings release and presentation on our investor relations website at noginc.com. Our Form 10-K will be filed with the SEC within the next several days. I'm joined this morning by our Chief Executive Officer, Nicholas O'Grady, our President, Adam Dirlam, our Chief Financial Officer, Chad Allen, and our Chief Technical Officer, James Evans. Our agenda for today's call is as follows. Nicholas will provide his remarks on the quarter and our recent accomplishments. Adam will give you an overview of operations and business development activities. Chad will review our financial results and walk through our 2024 guidance. After our prepared remarks, the team will be available to answer any questions.
Before we begin, let me go over our safe harbor language. Please be advised that our remarks today, including the answers to your questions, may include forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act. These forward-looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to be materially different from the expectations contemplated by our forward-looking statements. Those risks include, among others, matters that we have described in our earnings release as well as our filings with the SEC, including our annual report on Form 10-K and our quarterly reports on Form 10-Q. We disclaim any obligation to update these forward-looking statements. During today's call, we may discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures, including Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted Net Income, and Free Cash Flow. Reconciliations of these measures to the closest GAAP measures can be found in our earnings release.
With that, I will turn the call over to Nick.
Nicholas O'Grady

Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
I don't think it's gonna be material because there were also some mild curtailments in this Permian as well. I don't think it's gonna be. I mean on the margin, Donovan, I don't think it's gonna be. You know, you're talking about a 10-point difference between or seven point difference between the Permian and the rest of our oil basin. I don't think it's gonna be, you know, massive in any material way.
Operator
We'll move to our next question from Paul Diamond at Citi.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Good morning, all. Thanks for taking my call. Just a couple of quick ones. Talking about some outperformance on Forge. Can you just talk a bit more about that? You know, if you guys are seeing that as establishing the trend or I guess what you're expecting out of that this year.
James Evans
CTO, NOG
Yeah, thanks, Paul. This is Jim. Yeah, we're seeing the same thing. You know, Vital announced yesterday they're seeing about 30% to 35% outperformance on the new wells versus kind of the legacy Forge assets. We're seeing you know, something similar versus what we underwrote. It's around 30% outperformance. I think it's around you know, optimization on spacing, completion design, you know, production uptime on artificial lift. That is not baked into our go-forward plan. You know, we're still modeling based on what we originally underwrote for the acquisition. We do see you know, potential upside there. As we continue to go throughout the year, we think we'll see that and we'll adjust as we get more data.
Typically, we like to see 6 to 9 months of history before we feel confident in adjusting our assumptions. So far, we're very encouraged with what we're seeing out there.
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
Yeah. They've also just done, you know, one of their main initiatives when they bought the asset was really to work on the PDP itself, lowering costs of the actual oil BOE on the existing assets, and I think they've done a good job cleaning that up.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Got it. Understood. Just a quick follow-up. You have talked about having a lot of conversations with the SMID-cap operators. You talked about, you know, scale being similar to prior deals. Can you just dig down a bit more on that? Is there a pretty wide range to that scale you're seeing, or is it all pretty much locked in, you know, similar to, you know, Mascot, Forge, Novo, things of that sort? Or could we go a bit smaller, a bit larger? What are you guys seeing?
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
You mean just in terms of partners
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Yeah, exactly.
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
Yeah.
James Evans
CTO, NOG
It's all-
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Deal size and partners.
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
I mean, I think a lot of the stuff, you know, from the mega transactions, we have a lot of conversations with the largest of the large. Certainly, we have a lot of interest from small scale people as well who 'cause they always need money just like everybody else. I think in terms of the asset rationalization, we're also seeing the conversations from very large and mid-cap and upper mid-cap companies as well. I think it runs the gamut. I think what I would tell you from our perspective, and I'd rather let Adam talk about this than me, is that from our perspective, it's not a one size fits all.
Our methodology is going to change depending on what type of counterparty it is, meaning that we're going to adjust our structure based on what type of party it is. It's probably gonna become more mean-spirited depending on who we're dealing with.
Adam Dirlam
President, NOG
That's right. And just to, I guess, put it in perspective in terms of deal size and partners, I mean, on a ground game level, we're doing this on a unit-by-unit basis. We've also got, you know, for example, private equity groups that have just raised capital that are looking to, you know, participate in about the $100 to 200 million, you know, transaction size levels that are looking for a partner, so that they can use some of their dry powder for development on a go-forward basis. Then you've got, obviously, the ones that we executed last year, that were, you know, significantly larger than that. It runs the gamut, like Nick was saying.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Understood. Thanks for your time, and I'll leave it there.
Operator
We'll go next to John Abbott at Bank of America.
John Abbott
E&P Research VP, Bank of America
Hey, good morning, and thank you for taking our questions. Sticking with the forward of $6 billion of opportunities that you're seeing out there, and you look at the balance sheet, you look at your share price. I mean, what are your thoughts on potentially financing transactions at this point in time?
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
Yeah, I mean, John, we raised $290 million last fall, you know, for a reason, which was that we felt that we saw a great opportunity in front of us, and we wanted to be prepared to act. We've got over $1 billion of liquidity. Frankly, with all of the transactions that have happened, I think something like 10% of the revolvers have been recalled across the board. Chad is the most popular girl at the prom right now. He has banks begging him to take money. We certainly have capital available to us. I don't think that's the case for everybody, but I think for scaled companies like ourselves, the ability to raise additional capital is there.
Certainly, my point being that I think we have the capacity, you know, on balance sheet to, you know, for upwards of $1 billion, without raising any additional capital, and I think that would satiate us quite easily, you know, for the time being. Obviously, you know, beyond that, you know, we'll see. As you do those then. You know, we haven't really done much more than $1 billion in a year, so I think we're in pretty good shape for 2024.
John Abbott
E&P Research VP, Bank of America
Very, very helpful. I mean, there was a lot of conversations earlier on accrual accounting. I guess the real question here is, you know, looking beyond the noise as you sort of think about the exit rate for this year. You know-
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
Yeah.
Adam Dirlam
President, NOG
Nothing necessarily specific. Where do you kind of see the exit rate for 2024 in terms of production?
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
Yeah, I mean, as a non-operator, James Evans will stab me with a large knife if I talk about that because, you know, we just talked about how the timing can really vary. The truth is that if we see acceleration of projects and we see everything come on early in Q3, we'll produce a lot more barrels, and our guidance will be raised for the year. If we see our production peak in Q3, that would be a great thing. Theoretically, we'd see peak production in Q3, and your quote-unquote exit rate would be lower. Of course, we would find ways to redeploy capital and exit higher, so I'd be hesitant to see that.
I would say, as we described in our release, you know, we obviously believe we'll be down modestly in Q1. We would expect a material jump in Q2, another jump in Q3, and then, you know, a mild jump in Q4. I think, you know, that I would just leave it at that, for now. I would say that obviously based on our guidance, that is substantial, and I'm sorry to punt on that, but
Adam Dirlam
President, NOG
Well, it's February.
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
It's February.
Adam Dirlam
President, NOG
Things can change and come out of anywhere.
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
Yeah. I'm sorry, but as a non-operator, that's just the best I can do for you. I would say this, that like we're in the business to grow our company. You know, there's a reason in our business. Look, there are great things about being a non-operator, a lot of great things. But the timing of it, we know is the part of it. Honestly, to the extent that it gets accelerated, we're gonna produce a lot more barrels this year. That that's a good thing. But you know, the exit rate is. We're not a laundromat, right? You know, this is something, right, that it's not a machine.
The exit rate is sort of one of those things that people like to hang on to, but it's really about. It's not about a moment in time, it's about the number of barrels you produce over the life. I just say this, that we are in the business to grow the business over time, and I think that that's the most important thing.
John Abbott
E&P Research VP, Bank of America
Very helpful. Thank you for taking our questions.
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
Yep.
Operator
We'll take our final question from Noel Parks at Tuohy Brothers.
Noel Parks
Managing Director of CleanTech and E&P, Tuohy Brothers
Hi. Good morning. Just had a couple. You know, you talked a little earlier about you can't really do one size fits all in terms of just how you look at different acquisitions. Is it fair to say that you're pretty agnostic between private operated versus publicly traded operated non-op interest right now, either for the ground game or for larger M&A?
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
I wouldn't say that. I mean, I think it depends. It depends on the quality of the operator. I mean, there are great privates, but I'd say, you know, the largest, you know, there are really large operators that are bad. I mean, I think it just really goes operator specific. There are really good operators, and there are really bad operators that are big and small, right, Adam? I mean-
Adam Dirlam
President, NOG
Yeah. I think you need to differentiate what private means. Are you talking about private equity or are you talking about true private?
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
Yeah.
Adam Dirlam
President, NOG
Right? Those business models are run very, very differently.
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
Yeah.
Adam Dirlam
President, NOG
You know, you've got one that's renting an asset and one that's had it and will continue to have it for a very, very long time. Their viewpoint on a short-term or a long-term basis could be very, very different.
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
Yeah. I mean, Mewbourne is a private company, and it's one of the finest operators in the world. You know, I can think of many private equity backed operators that are, you know, renting the asset and looking to flip it.
Adam Dirlam
President, NOG
Yeah. I mean, I would say typically we're looking at people who have a similar view as us in terms of the long term, but that's not to say that there aren't great private equity operators that are out there as well that we'd be willing to partner with.
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
Absolutely.
Noel Parks
Managing Director of CleanTech and E&P, Tuohy Brothers
Oh, great. Well, thanks for the clarification. I guess I was wondering a bit, talking about the Williston, and we have seen a deal there, the first one maybe in quite a while of any size. Just wondering, I have not paid a lot of attention to the state of sort of the land management out there. You know, leases, some of those leases are probably 15 years old, if not longer at this point. I just wonder, you know, you've been there so long, are things pretty cleaned up there, or is there still stuff to do just in terms of, I don't know, you know, neglected books or, you know, absent non-op positions that you can still, you know, still
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
It's pretty blocked up, Noel, but there are still, you know, things to do. I mean, you know, it's just gonna be more about people when they're ready. There are things that are owned that when people are ready to sell, will be sold. But I don't think it's like the Wild West where there's lots of open land ready to be sold. Is that fair, Adam?
Adam Dirlam
President, NOG
Yeah, I think that's fair. The other thing that I would add to that is just the evolution of the completion methodology, right? You've seen a lot of operators, you know, refine those techniques and step out. The rate of return and the economics on some of those projects that you wouldn't even look at, you know, call it two, three years ago, are things that are certainly viable now. That changes the landscape from a land standpoint. You can do some of the blocking and tackling in terms of picking up some white space acreage and bringing in appropriate operators that you know are gonna do a good job. As a non-operator, you know, we're not beholden to one particular area, right?
We can get into the core day in and day out and continue to gross up our working interest as we get, you know, 100 AFEs a quarter, as we did in 2023. There's always wood to chop. It just is a different dynamic.
Operator
That concludes the question and answer session. I would like to turn the conference over to Nicholas O'Grady for closing remarks.
Nicholas O'Grady
CEO, NOG
Thanks everyone for joining us today. We'll see you on the next one. Appreciate your time. This is the way.
Operator
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
